title: Two Creation Accounts, Eden and Babel
bigQuestion: What do we notice when we read the opening chapters of Genesis slowly, word by word, and how have Jewish, Christian and academic readers explained what they found?

story.title: Two Colors of Ink
story.kicker: Two students take the first three chapters of Genesis and underline every name for God. The pattern they find is one that readers have argued about for more than a century.
paragraphs: Maya and Jordan sit at a library table in Rogers Park with two copies of Genesis, one blue pen and one red pen. Their teacher gave them one job: read Genesis 1 through 3 and underline every name for God. Blue for the word "God" by itself. Red for "LORD God," printed with LORD in small capital letters. They think it will take ten minutes.

Genesis 1 goes fast. "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." Blue. "And God said, Let there be light." Blue. By the end of the seventh day, Maya has underlined the word God about thirty-five times, and there is not one red mark on the page. The chapter is orderly, almost like a list. Each day begins, God speaks, the thing appears, God sees that it is good, and evening and morning close the day.

Then Jordan reaches Genesis 2:4, and the pen changes hands. "In the day that the LORD God made the earth and the heavens." Red. From here to the end of chapter 3, nearly every line is red. And the story itself feels different. There is no seven-day list. A man is formed from dust before any plants grow. A garden is planted. Animals are made after the man, and a woman is formed last of all. The order in chapter 1 was plants, animals, then people together.

Maya flips back and forth. "It's like two different writers," she says. Jordan is not so sure. "Or one writer who wanted two views of the same event. A wide shot and then a close-up." They have, without knowing it, just restated a debate that has run since the 1700s. Jewish and Christian readers noticed the two names long ago and explained them one way. Modern scholars noticed the same names and explained them another way.

This chapter hands you the same two pens. You will read Genesis 1 and 2 side by side, learn the names of the different explanations, put Genesis beside a Babylonian creation poem, and then follow the text through Eden, Cain and Abel, the flood and the tower of Babel. The goal is not to decide who is right. The goal is to see what is on the page, and to understand why careful readers see it differently.
story.think: Maya says two writers; Jordan says one writer with two views. What evidence from the page would you need to decide between them, and could the evidence support both?

lessons.title: The Shape of Genesis 1
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 1:1–2:3 is built on repetition: a seven-day frame, a set formula for each day, and a refrain that God saw it was good.
reading: Genesis 1:1–2:3 is one of the most patterned passages in the Bible. Read it aloud and the *structure* shows itself. Each day follows the same steps. God speaks ("And God said"). The thing comes to be ("and it was so"). God names or blesses it. God sees that it is good. Then a closing line: "And the evening and the morning were the first day." The same *formula* repeats six times, and the seventh day breaks the pattern by having no work at all.

Readers have long noticed a second pattern inside the first. Days one to three make spaces: light and dark, sky and sea, dry land with plants. Days four to six fill those spaces in the same order: sun, moon and stars for the light; birds and fish for sky and sea; land animals and people for the land. Many scholars call this a "framework" reading. Jewish and Christian commentators from the Middle Ages had already observed that the days come in matched pairs.

The chapter's key words repeat too. The word for God here is the Hebrew *Elohim*, which appears about thirty-five times in these thirty-four verses. "And God said" comes ten times. "Good" comes seven times, ending with "very good." Repetition in an ancient text is rarely an accident. It is a way of stressing what matters, and it is the first tool in a close reader's kit: count what repeats, then ask why.

words.d: the way a passage is built and ordered; its parts and how they fit together
a fixed set of words that a text repeats on purpose, like "and it was so"
the Hebrew word for God used all through Genesis 1; it is grammatically plural but takes a singular verb

look.title: What repeats in Genesis 1:1–2:3
look.cite: Counted in the King James Version (1611), Genesis 1:1–2:3; counts vary slightly by translation
look.prompt: Which of these numbers surprises you least, and which one would you point to if you were arguing that the passage was written to be recited aloud?

check.q: Which step is part of the repeated formula for each day in Genesis 1?
choices: God speaks and the thing comes to be
A man is formed from dust
A river divides into four heads
check.why: Each day in Genesis 1 opens with "And God said" and the thing appears. Dust, rivers and the serpent belong to Genesis 2–3.

check.q: In the framework reading, what do days four to six do?
choices: Undo the work of days one to three
Fill the spaces made on days one to three
Repeat days one to three word for word
check.why: Days one to three make light, sky and sea, and land; days four to six fill them with lights, birds and fish, and land creatures.

check.q: What is the Hebrew name for God used throughout Genesis 1?
check.why: Genesis 1:1–2:3 uses Elohim, translated "God," about thirty-five times; the four-letter name appears only from Genesis 2:4.

lessons.title: The Garden Account
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 2:4–3:24 tells of creation again, in a different order and a different style, centered on a garden, a man, a woman and a command.
reading: At Genesis 2:4 the text says, "These are the generations of the heavens and of the earth," and begins again. This time there is no count of days. The ground is dry and empty because no rain has fallen. Then the text says God formed a man from the dust of the ground and breathed life into him. Only afterward does God plant a *garden* in Eden and set the man in it, with one command: eat from every tree except the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

The order matters to close readers. In Genesis 1 the plants come on day three, the animals on days five and six, and people last, male and female together. In Genesis 2 the man comes first, then the plants, then the animals, which the man names, and last the woman, built from the man's side. The style is different too. Genesis 1 is formal and repetitive. Genesis 2–3 is a *narrative* with scenes, dialogue and suspense: a talking serpent, a fruit, a hiding couple, a question in the cool of the evening.

Chapter 3 ends the account with judgment and exile. The serpent is cursed, the woman is told of pain in childbirth, the man is told the ground will resist him, and both are sent out of the garden. Cherubim and a flaming sword guard the way back to the tree of life. Read as a piece of writing, Genesis 2–3 has a clear arc: a gift, a rule, a test, a choice, a loss. What it means is the work of the next section. What it says is the work of this one.

words.d: the enclosed, watered place in Eden where Genesis 2 sets the first man and woman
a story told in scenes with characters, speech and events in sequence
Hebrew for "generations" or "what came from"; the formula that opens new sections of Genesis about ten times

look.title: The forming of the man
look.text: And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
look.prompt: Compare this verse with Genesis 1:27, where God creates humans "in his own image." What does each verse stress about what a human being is?

check.q: In Genesis 2, what is made first?
check.why: Genesis 2:7 forms the man from dust before the garden is planted (2:8) and before the animals (2:19) and the woman (2:22).

check.q: Which feature belongs to the style of Genesis 2–3 rather than Genesis 1?
check.why: Genesis 2–3 is narrative, with speech and scenes; the seven-day count, refrain and paired days belong to Genesis 1.

check.q: What does the phrase "These are the generations" (toledot) do in Genesis?
check.why: The toledot formula appears about ten times in Genesis and marks the start of a new section, including at 2:4.

lessons.title: Two Names, Two Voices
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 1 calls God Elohim; Genesis 2–3 calls God YHWH Elohim, printed LORD God; readers explain that shift in very different ways.
reading: Open the King James Version or the 1917 Jewish Publication Society Tanakh and you will see "God" in Genesis 1 and "LORD God" in Genesis 2–3, with LORD in small capitals. The small capitals are a signal. They mark the four Hebrew letters YHWH, called the *Tetragrammaton*. Jewish practice for many centuries has been not to pronounce this name, saying *Adonai* ("my Lord") instead. English translators followed that custom and printed LORD.

The shift in names is old news to the tradition. A rabbinic collection called Genesis Rabbah, compiled in the early centuries of the Common Era, reads Elohim as the name that shows God's justice and YHWH as the name that shows God's mercy. On that reading, Genesis 1 shows the world made by justice, and Genesis 2 adds mercy so that the world can stand. Many medieval Jewish and Christian commentators followed this path: one author, two names, chosen on purpose.

Modern scholars starting in the 1700s took the same clue and drew a different map. A French physician, Jean Astruc, proposed in 1753 that Moses had used older written sources, one favoring Elohim and one favoring YHWH. Later scholars turned this into a theory of separate documents. The next section explains it. For now, notice the method. Both the rabbis and the scholars began by counting names, exactly as Maya and Jordan did with their two pens.

words.d: the four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH, printed as LORD in small capitals in most English Bibles
Hebrew for "my Lord"; the word Jewish readers say aloud in place of the four-letter name
rabbinic interpretation of Scripture that fills gaps and explains details; Genesis Rabbah is one collection

look.title: Two verses, two names
look.text: Genesis 1:27 (KJV): "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them." Genesis 2:7 (KJV): "And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." Genesis Rabbah reads the first name as justice and the second as mercy. A documentary scholar reads the first as one source and the second as another.
look.prompt: Take one of the two readings and explain how it accounts for the change in verbs too: "created" in 1:27 and "formed" and "breathed" in 2:7.

check.q: What do the small capitals in LORD signal in the King James Version?
check.why: Translators print LORD in small capitals wherever the Hebrew has the four-letter name YHWH, following the Jewish custom of saying Adonai.

check.q: How does Genesis Rabbah explain the two names for God?
choices: As two authors writing in different centuries
As names showing justice and mercy
As names of two different gods
check.why: The midrash reads Elohim as the name of justice and YHWH as the name of mercy, both belonging to one God and one author.

check.q: Jean Astruc's 1753 proposal was that
choices: the two names mark two Hebrew dialects
Genesis 1 was added in the Middle Ages
Moses used older sources that favored different names
check.why: Astruc suggested Moses had drawn on earlier written sources, one using Elohim and one using YHWH; later scholars built on this.

lessons.title: The Documentary Hypothesis
lessons.mainIdea: Many scholars since the 1800s have explained the Torah as a weave of four written sources, labeled J, E, D and P, combined by later editors.
reading: The *documentary hypothesis* is the name for a scholarly theory about how the Torah was written. Its classic form was set out by the German scholar Julius Wellhausen in his Prolegomena to the History of Israel (1878). Wellhausen argued that four separate written sources had been joined by editors over several centuries. He labeled them with letters: J, E, D and P.

J is the Yahwist (spelled with a J in German), the source that uses the name YHWH from the beginning and tells vivid stories like the garden of Eden. E is the Elohist, which prefers Elohim and is thought to come from the northern kingdom of Israel. D is the Deuteronomist, mostly the book of Deuteronomy with its speeches and its call to worship in one place. P is the Priestly source, with its interest in order, genealogies, dates and ritual; Genesis 1 is the standard example. Wellhausen dated P last, after the exile of the 500s BCE.

Scholars who use this model point to evidence like the two creation accounts, two flood stories that seem to be spliced together (two of every animal in Genesis 6:19, but seven pairs of clean animals in 7:2), and differences in vocabulary and style. They call the person or people who combined the sources the *redactor*. The hypothesis is a theory, not a discovery of actual scrolls. No manuscript of J or P has ever been found. It stands or falls on how well it explains the text we have.

words.d: the theory that the Torah was assembled from several earlier written sources
an editor who combines and arranges earlier texts into a finished work
the proposed source (P) marked by lists, dates, genealogies and ritual; Genesis 1 is its usual example
the proposed source (J) that uses the name YHWH and tells vivid stories such as Eden

look.title: Landmarks in the study of the Torah's sources
rows: De Wette links Deuteronomy to Josiah's reform
Rendtorff's challenge to the four-source model
look.cite: Standard histories of biblical scholarship; dates of first publication
look.prompt: The theory has been argued over for more than 250 years. What does that tell you about how hard the evidence is to settle?

check.q: Which source does the documentary hypothesis usually assign Genesis 1 to?
check.why: Genesis 1's order, formulas and interest in the seventh day are the classic marks scholars attribute to P.

check.q: What is a redactor?
choices: A prophet who speaks for God
An editor who joins earlier texts
A scribe who copies one scroll
check.why: In the hypothesis, a redactor combined J, E, D and P into the Torah we have.

check.q: Which statement about the documentary hypothesis is accurate?
choices: Scrolls of J and P were found near the Dead Sea
It is a theory built on features of the text, not on found manuscripts
It says Moses wrote all four sources
check.why: No manuscript of any proposed source exists; the theory rests on doublets, names and style within the received text.

lessons.title: Tradition and the Critics
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish and Christian tradition names Moses as the Torah's author, and both religious readers and academic scholars have challenged the four-source model.
reading: For most of history, Jewish and Christian readers held that Moses wrote the Torah, the five books from Genesis to Deuteronomy. Later books of the Bible refer to "the book of Moses" and "the law of Moses." Many Orthodox Jews and many Christians today hold to *Mosaic authorship* as a matter of faith. A few medieval commentators, such as Abraham ibn Ezra in the 1100s, hinted that some verses came from a later hand. They did not doubt the whole.

Critics of the documentary hypothesis come from more than one direction. The Italian Jewish scholar Umberto Cassuto argued in lectures in 1941 that the shift between Elohim and YHWH follows the meaning of each passage, not separate authors, much as Genesis Rabbah had said. In the 1970s academic scholars such as Rolf Rendtorff argued that the Torah grew from smaller blocks of tradition rather than four long documents. Others defend a *supplementary* model: one base text expanded over time.

Where does that leave a student? With a text and a set of competing maps. Most university scholars today still speak of P and D as recognizable layers, while J and E are debated more than they once were. Religious readers may accept, adapt or reject any of this. The classroom task is narrower: know what each reading claims, what evidence it uses, and what it cannot explain. That is what it means to read a *canon*, a collection a community has received as Scripture, with both respect and care.

words.d: the traditional view that Moses wrote the five books of the Torah
the view that one base text was expanded by later additions rather than woven from separate documents
the list of books a religious community accepts as its Scripture

look.title: Three maps of one text
look.text: Map A (tradition): Moses wrote the Torah; the two names for God show two sides of God's character. Map B (Wellhausen): four documents, J, E, D and P, were joined by editors; the names mark different sources. Map C (Cassuto): one author chose each name to fit the passage, so the pattern is literary, not a seam. All three agree on what the page says. They disagree about why.
look.prompt: Pick one fact from Genesis 1–3 (a name, an order, a repeated phrase) and explain how each map would account for it. Which map has the hardest time with your fact?

check.q: What did Umberto Cassuto argue about the names of God?
choices: They were added by Greek translators
They follow the meaning of each passage
check.why: Cassuto's 1941 lectures held that one author chose Elohim or YHWH to fit the content, not that separate sources were spliced.

check.q: Mosaic authorship means
choices: Moses copied the Torah from Babylon
Moses wrote the five books of the Torah
check.why: Mosaic authorship is the traditional Jewish and Christian view that Moses wrote Genesis through Deuteronomy.

check.q: A supplementary model of the Torah holds that
choices: four equal documents were woven together
the text was translated from Aramaic
one base text was expanded over time
the Torah was written in a single year
check.why: Supplementary models describe growth by addition to a core text, in contrast to the four-document weave.

lessons.title: Genesis Beside Babylon
lessons.mainIdea: Enuma Elish, a Babylonian creation poem, shares images with Genesis 1 but tells a very different kind of story, and readers weigh the likeness in different ways.
reading: In 1876 George Smith of the British Museum published tablets from the library of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal at Nineveh. On them, in cuneiform, was a Babylonian poem now called *Enuma Elish*, from its opening words, "When on high." Its date of composition is debated. Many scholars place it in the late second millennium BCE. That is earlier than most dates given for the writing of Genesis 1. Its discovery changed how people read the Bible's first page.

The poem tells how the young god Marduk fights the sea goddess Tiamat, kills her, and splits her body to make the sky and the earth. He then has humans made from the blood of a defeated god so that they can do the gods' work. Readers noticed likenesses to Genesis: a watery beginning, a dividing of waters, a sequence ending in humans, and a rest for the gods. Some scholars connect the Hebrew word for "the deep," *tehom*, in Genesis 1:2 with the name Tiamat. Others say the words are simply related and no borrowing is needed.

The differences are as striking as the likenesses. Genesis 1 has no battle, no rival gods and no birth of God. God speaks and the world is. Humans are made "in the image of God," not as servants from a corpse. Many scholars therefore read Genesis 1 as a deliberate answer to stories like Enuma Elish, using the shared *cosmology* of the ancient Near East to say something new. Jewish and Christian readers have generally agreed that the contrast is the point, whatever they think about the source of the likeness.

words.d: the Babylonian creation poem, named from its first words, "When on high"
wedge-shaped writing pressed into clay, used across ancient Mesopotamia
a picture of how the universe is put together; the ancient one had waters above and below a flat earth
Hebrew for "the deep," the dark waters of Genesis 1:2

look.title: Marduk divides the sea
look.text: In the poem's fourth tablet, Marduk defeats Tiamat with wind and arrow, then splits her body in two like a fish for drying. With one half he makes the sky and sets a bar so its waters cannot escape. In the sixth tablet, the gods make humans from the blood of Tiamat's ally Kingu, so that the gods may rest.
look.cite: Enuma Elish, tablets IV and VI, paraphrased from the cuneiform text published by George Smith (1876) and later editions
look.prompt: List two details here that have a counterpart in Genesis 1 and two that have none. What is the effect of the missing pieces?

check.q: Who published the tablets of Enuma Elish in 1876?
check.why: George Smith of the British Museum published the Nineveh tablets; Wellhausen, Astruc and Cassuto worked on the Torah's sources.

check.q: Which element is found in Enuma Elish but not in Genesis 1?
check.why: Both texts begin with waters and divide them and both make humans; only the Babylonian poem has a combat between Marduk and Tiamat.

check.q: How do many scholars describe the relationship between the two texts?
choices: Genesis 1 copied the poem word for word
The poem was written after Genesis to mock it
The two are unrelated in every way
Genesis 1 uses a shared world-picture to say something different
check.why: The common view is that Genesis 1 shares an ancient cosmology but answers the combat story with a creation by speech alone.

lessons.title: Eden Read as Story
lessons.mainIdea: Read as narrative, Genesis 3 is full of deliberate gaps, and noticing what the text does not say is a close-reading skill.
reading: A story can be read for what it says and for what it leaves out. Genesis 3 leaves out a great deal. The *serpent* is called the most subtle of the beasts, but the text never says it is evil, never explains why it talks, and never names it Satan. That identification comes later, in Jewish and Christian writings from the last centuries BCE onward. The fruit is never called an apple; that idea grows from a Latin pun between malum (evil) and malum (apple).

Notice too what the serpent says. It asks whether God really forbade every tree, and the woman corrects it. Then it says, "Ye shall not surely die," and promises that their eyes will be opened and they will be as gods, knowing good and evil. The text lets the reader weigh who is telling the truth. The couple do not die that day. Their eyes are opened. They also lose the garden. A close reader marks this as a *gap*, a place where the text expects you to think.

The book of Genesis itself never returns to Eden to explain it. The prophets rarely mention it. So the meaning of Genesis 3 has been supplied by its readers, and the next lesson shows how differently they have done so. Before the interpretation, it helps to fix the plain events: a command, a question, a bite, a covering of fig leaves, a hiding, a questioning, three judgments and an exit east of Eden. Everything else is reading.

words.d: the talking snake of Genesis 3; the text calls it subtle and does not name it further
something a story leaves unsaid on purpose, inviting the reader to fill it in
reading slowly and carefully, attending to each word, repetition, order and silence

look.title: The serpent's promise
look.text: For God doth know that in the day ye eat thereof, then your eyes shall be opened, and ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil.
look.prompt: Genesis 3:7 says their eyes were opened, and 3:22 has God say the man has become "as one of us, to know good and evil." Was the serpent lying? Use only what the text says.

check.q: Which detail is actually stated in Genesis 3?
choices: The serpent is the most subtle of the beasts
check.why: Genesis 3:1 calls the serpent subtle; the names Satan and apple come from later readers and a Latin pun.

check.q: In close reading, a gap is
choices: a missing page in a manuscript
something the story leaves unsaid on purpose
check.why: A gap is a deliberate silence that invites the reader to think, such as why the serpent can talk.

check.q: Where does the idea of the apple come from?
check.why: Latin malum means both "evil" and "apple"; the Hebrew text says only "fruit."

lessons.title: Eden as Theology and Allegory
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish, Christian and Muslim readers draw different lessons from Eden, and some in every tradition have read it as allegory rather than as literal history.
reading: Christians have often read Genesis 3 as "the Fall," a phrase that is not in Genesis. The reading rests largely on Paul's letter to the Romans, chapter 5, which says that sin entered the world through one man. Augustine of Hippo, around 400 CE, developed this into the doctrine of *original sin*: every human inherits a damaged nature from Adam. Eastern Orthodox Christians speak instead of "ancestral sin," inheriting death and weakness but not guilt. These are differences within Christianity, and both sides cite the same chapter.

Jewish tradition, reading the same text, did not develop a doctrine of original sin. Rabbinic writings speak of a human "inclination" to evil and to good, both present in every person from the start. Each person answers for their own choices. Eden in Jewish reading is more often about exile and return, or about the cost of knowledge, than about inherited guilt. The Qur'an tells of Adam and his wife in a garden too. Muslims read that Adam repented and God forgave him. In Islam Adam is the first prophet, not the source of a fallen nature.

Some readers in every tradition have treated Eden as *allegory*, a story whose figures stand for something else. Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish writer of the first century CE, read the garden as a picture of the soul. The Christian teacher Origen, in the 200s, asked who could take literally a God who walks in a garden in the evening. Others insist on a plain, historical reading. John Milton's Paradise Lost (1667) retold the story as an epic and shaped how English readers imagine it. A public classroom presents all of these as readings, and takes none as the verdict.

words.d: the Christian doctrine, shaped by Augustine, that all humans inherit a damaged nature from Adam
a reading in which the people and things in a story stand for ideas
in rabbinic thought, the pull toward evil (yetzer ha-ra) and toward good (yetzer ha-tov) in every person

look.title: Four readers at one tree
look.text: Augustine (Christian, c. 400 CE): Adam's sin is passed to all people; only grace repairs it. A rabbinic reader: every person has two inclinations and answers for their own deeds; Eden is the first exile. A Muslim reader: Adam slipped, repented and was forgiven; he is the first prophet. Philo (Jewish, 1st century CE): the garden is the soul, the serpent is pleasure, and the story is about the inner life.
look.prompt: Which of these readers would find Genesis 3:22–24, the exile from the garden, most important, and why? Which reader is least interested in whether the events happened?

check.q: Which Christian thinker shaped the doctrine of original sin?
check.why: Augustine, around 400 CE, built the doctrine on Romans 5; Philo was a Jewish allegorist, Milton a poet, Wellhausen a source critic.

check.q: How does rabbinic tradition tend to read Eden?
choices: As a story of exile and personal responsibility
As a text to be removed from the Torah
check.why: Jewish tradition speaks of two inclinations in each person and reads Eden as exile and the cost of knowledge, not inherited guilt.

check.q: In Islamic reading, Adam is
choices: the source of a fallen nature
a figure absent from the Qur'an
the first prophet, forgiven after repenting
check.why: Muslims read that Adam repented and was forgiven, and count him as the first prophet.

lessons.title: Cain and Abel
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 4 tells the first murder in a few spare verses, and its unexplained choices have made it a model text for reading gaps.
reading: Genesis 4 moves fast. Eve bears Cain, then Abel. Abel keeps sheep; Cain works the ground. Each brings an *offering*, and the text says God had respect for Abel's offering but not for Cain's. It never says why. Readers have proposed reasons for two thousand years: Abel brought the firstborn and the fat, Cain brought merely "of the fruit"; or Cain's heart was wrong; or the text is teaching that God's choice is free. The gap is the point.

God speaks to Cain before the crime, telling him that sin crouches at the door like an animal, wanting him, but that he can master it. Cain talks with Abel in the field and kills him. Then comes one of the most quoted exchanges in the Bible. God asks where Abel is. Cain answers with a question of his own: "Am I my brother's keeper?" The text says the blood cries from the ground, and Cain is sent to wander, but with a *mark* that protects him from being killed in turn.

Notice the structure. Genesis 3 had a command, a wrong, a question from God, an answer that shifts blame, a judgment and an exile east of Eden. Genesis 4 repeats every step. Many scholars read this as a deliberate echo, the story of the first family told twice at growing scale. Jewish tradition draws from the plural "bloods" in the Hebrew of 4:10 the teaching that to destroy one life is to destroy a whole world. Christian writers have read Abel as the first martyr. The verse itself remains a question with no answer given.

words.d: a gift brought to God; in Genesis 4, grain from Cain and firstborn sheep from Abel
the unexplained sign God puts on Cain so that no one will kill him
a later passage that repeats the pattern of an earlier one, inviting comparison

look.title: The question in the field
look.text: And the LORD said unto Cain, Where is Abel thy brother? And he said, I know not: Am I my brother's keeper?
look.prompt: Compare God's question here with the question to Adam in Genesis 3:9, "Where art thou?" What does asking a question, rather than accusing, do in each scene?

check.q: What reason does Genesis 4 give for God's preferring Abel's offering?
choices: None; the text does not say
check.why: The text states only that God had respect for Abel's offering and not Cain's; the reasons come from later readers.

check.q: The mark of Cain in Genesis 4 is
choices: a sign that protects him from being killed
check.why: Genesis 4:15 says the mark is set so that anyone finding Cain will not kill him.

check.q: Why do many scholars call Genesis 4 an echo of Genesis 3?
choices: Both follow the same steps: wrong, question, blame, judgment, exile
check.why: The two chapters share a structure, from God's question to an exile eastward, told at a larger scale in chapter 4.

lessons.title: The Flood and Gilgamesh
lessons.mainIdea: The flood story in Genesis 6–9 has close parallels in Mesopotamian texts, and its own doubled details have fueled the source debate.
reading: In 1872 George Smith stood before a London audience and read from a broken clay tablet. It told of a man warned by a god to build a boat, load it with animals, and survive a great flood, and of birds sent out to find dry land. The tablet was part of the Epic of *Gilgamesh*, tablet XI, and the survivor's name was Utnapishtim. An older Babylonian version, Atrahasis, has since been found too. The likeness to Noah's story in Genesis 6–9 was immediately clear.

Genesis tells its own version with its own concerns. God sees the earth filled with violence and decides to send a flood. Noah is told to build an *ark* and bring the animals. Rain falls forty days. The waters prevail one hundred and fifty days. Noah sends a raven and then a dove, which returns with an olive leaf. After the flood God makes a *covenant*, a binding promise, never again to destroy the earth by flood, and sets the rainbow as its sign. Unlike the Mesopotamian gods, who send the flood because humans are noisy, the God of Genesis acts against violence and then binds himself by a promise.

The Genesis flood is also a favorite example for the documentary hypothesis. Noah takes two of every animal in 6:19–20 but seven pairs of clean animals in 7:2. The rain lasts forty days in 7:12, but the waters rise for one hundred and fifty days in 7:24. Source critics see two accounts, J and P, spliced together. Readers like Cassuto answer that the numbers describe different stages of one event and that the doubling is a style of ancient storytelling. The student's job, again, is to see the data first and the theory second.

check.q: Which ancient text contains a flood story with a survivor named Utnapishtim?
check.why: Tablet XI of Gilgamesh tells the flood; Enuma Elish is a creation poem and Hammurabi's text is a law collection.

check.q: What sign does Genesis 9 attach to God's covenant after the flood?
check.why: Genesis 9:13 sets the bow in the cloud as the token of the covenant; the dove and olive leaf come earlier in the story.

It gives doubled details, like two and seven of the animals

lessons.title: Babel and the Toolkit
lessons.mainIdea: The tower of Babel story uses wordplay and mirrored structure, and it models the close-reading toolkit: repetition, keyword, structure and gap.
reading: Genesis 11:1–9 is nine verses long and built like a mirror. People move east, find a plain in Shinar, and say, "Let us make brick" and "Let us build us a city and a tower." Then God says, "Let us go down" and confuses their language. The people's "let us" is answered by God's "let us." Their plan to make a name is answered by scattering. The place is named *Babel*, and the text explains the name with a *pun*: it sounds like the Hebrew verb balal, "to confuse." Babylonian speakers heard their city's name as "gate of the god."

Scholars connect the tower to the *ziggurat*, the stepped temple towers of Mesopotamian cities, whose tops were said to reach heaven. Read that way, the story is a Hebrew author's comment on the great city of Babylon. Jewish and Christian readers have read the tower as pride punished, or as the origin of the world's languages, or as a warning about empires that erase difference. Genesis itself gives no verdict word like "pride." It reports what the builders said and what God did.

Babel closes the first part of Genesis, and it is a good place to gather the tools this chapter has used. Repetition: count what recurs ("and God said"; "let us"). Keyword: watch a loaded word (name, good, know). Structure: map the shape (days paired; two exiles east; a mirror). Gap: mark what is not said (why Abel; who the serpent is). Use all four on any passage in the Torah and you will be reading the way careful readers of every tradition have read for two thousand years.

check.q: How does Genesis 11 explain the name Babel?
choices: By a pun on the Hebrew for "confuse"
check.why: Genesis 11:9 links Babel to balal, "to confuse"; "gate of the god" is what the name meant in Babylonian.

check.q: A ziggurat is
choices: a stepped temple tower in Mesopotamia
check.why: Ziggurats were the stepped towers of Mesopotamian cities and are the likely background of the Babel story.

check.q: Which item is one of the four close-reading tools in this chapter?
choices: Gap: noticing what the text does not say
check.why: The toolkit is repetition, keyword, structure and gap; gaps are the silences a story leaves for the reader.

review.q: Which name for God is used throughout Genesis 1:1–2:3?
review.why: Genesis 1 uses Elohim about thirty-five times; "LORD God" (YHWH Elohim) begins at 2:4.

review.q: In which order are people, plants and animals made in Genesis 2?
review.why: Genesis 2 forms the man first, then plants the garden, then makes animals, and builds the woman last.

review.q: The letters J, E, D and P stand for
choices: four proposed written sources of the Torah
review.why: In the documentary hypothesis they are the Yahwist, Elohist, Deuteronomist and Priestly sources.

review.q: Genesis Rabbah explains the two names of God as
review.why: The midrash reads Elohim as the name of justice and YHWH as the name of mercy.

review.q: What does Enuma Elish have that Genesis 1 lacks?
choices: A combat between gods and humans made from a god's blood
review.why: Genesis 1 shares the watery beginning, division and rest, but has no battle and makes humans in God's image.

review.q: Which tradition speaks of "ancestral sin" rather than inherited guilt?
review.why: Eastern Orthodox Christians use "ancestral sin" for inherited death and weakness without inherited guilt.

review.q: In Genesis 7, what pair of numbers do source critics point to?
choices: Six days and one day of rest
Two of every animal and seven pairs of clean animals
review.why: Genesis 6:19–20 says two of each and 7:2 says seven pairs of clean animals; critics read this as two sources.

review.q: Which close-reading tool would you use to notice that Genesis 3 never explains why the serpent can talk?
review.why: A gap is what a story leaves unsaid on purpose; the serpent's speech is one of the famous gaps of Genesis 3.
